In 2008, British science writer and alternative medicine skeptic Simon Singh wrote an opinion article for the Guardian entitled "Beware the Spinal Tap," in which he criticized the British Chiropractic Association for supporting junk science. He wrote:

The British Chiropractic Association claims that their members can help treat children with colic, sleeping and feeding problems, frequent ear infections, asthma and prolonged crying, even though there is not a jot of evidence. This organisation is the respectable face of the chiropractic profession and yet it happily promotes bogus treatments.

and was promptly sued by the BCA for libel. If he lived in the United States, the courts would be equally as quick in dismissing the case as over-litigious nonsense. However, in the UK, libel laws are far more plaintiff-friendly. They are so plaintiff-friendly that they actually put the burden of proof on the accused to prove that the claims made are not libelous. Guilty until proven innocent, if you will. Singh spent the next several years in an arduous and costly legal battle to defend his right to freely criticize an organization that he disagrees with. He eventually won, but ended up spending Â£20,000 of his own money in the process--a cost so prohibitive that even blatantly specious libel cases are often settled out of court in the UK. Monied interests have the ability to bully individuals into retracting legitimate criticism.

It is this very system that Republican front-runner Donald Trump wants to model the US system after. What he fails to tell you is that this would require an amendment to the Constitution. According to legal precedent, Trump's proposal would be a serious abridgment of First Amendment rights. In the US, the plaintiff needs to prove that the statement was not only false but that it was made with malicious intent. This requirement is necessary to preserve free speech, encourage open debate, and protect law-abiding citizens from costly litigation.
